title: Der Mond
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 175. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, hieng, ward).
about: An origin story explaining why the moon exists and why it wanes and waxes: four young men steal a lamp-like moon from a neighboring land, and each keeps a quarter of it as he dies, until the pieces are reunited in the underworld and eventually hung in the sky by St Peter. It reads as one of the Grimms’ folk etiologies, closer to legend than fairy tale, and pairs naturally with KHM 176 on the span of life. Watch for the older forms gieng, ward and hieng, common across this stretch of the collection.

sentences.t: Vorzeiten gab es ein Land, wo die Nacht immer dunkel und der Himmel wie ein schwarzes Tuch darüber gebreitet war, denn es gieng dort niemals der Mond auf, und kein Stern blinkte in der Finsternis.
sentences.l: In former times there was a land where the night was always dark and the sky was spread over it like a black cloth, for there the moon never rose, and no star gleamed in the darkness.
sentences.i: Long ago there was a land where the night was always dark and the sky lay spread over it like a black cloth, for the moon never rose there, and no star gleamed in the gloom.
sentences.n: “Vorzeiten” — in olden times; this tale opens with it instead of the usual “Es war einmal.” “gieng … auf” is aufgehen, to rise (of a heavenly body): a separable verb whose particle auf waits at the end of the clause. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging, and you will meet the -ie- spelling throughout (fieng, hieng).

sentences.t: Bei Erschaffung der Welt hatte das nächtliche Licht ausgereicht.
sentences.l: At the creation of the world the nightly light had sufficed.
sentences.i: At the making of the world the light of the night had been just enough.
sentences.n: One flat sentence carries the whole explanation, and its sense is arguable: “ausgereicht” (ausreichen, to suffice) can be read as ‘the light allotted for night had been enough — and no more was ever given’, or as ‘it had only gone so far, and did not stretch to this land.’ The German leaves it open and so does the English here.

sentences.t: Aus diesem Land giengen einmal vier Bursche auf die Wanderschaft und gelangten in ein anderes Reich, wo Abends, wenn die Sonne hinter den Bergen verschwunden war, auf einem Eichbaum eine leuchtende Kugel stand, die weit und breit ein sanftes Licht ausgoß.
sentences.l: Out of this land four lads once went on their travels and came into another realm, where in the evening, when the sun had vanished behind the mountains, on an oak tree a shining globe stood, which poured out a soft light far and wide.
sentences.i: Out of this land four lads once set off on their travels and came to another realm where, in the evening, when the sun had gone down behind the mountains, a shining globe stood on an oak tree and poured a gentle light far and wide.
sentences.n: “auf die Wanderschaft gehen” is the journeyman’s road: a young craftsman travelled from town to town for a few years before he could set up on his own, so four lads on the move is an everyday sight, not an adventure. The globe “stood” on the tree, as a lamp stands on its bracket.

sentences.t: Man konnte dabei alles wohl sehen und unterscheiden, wenn es auch nicht so glänzend wie die Sonne war.
sentences.l: One could see and distinguish everything well by it, even if it was not so brilliant as the sun.
sentences.i: By its light one could see and make out everything well enough, though it was not so brilliant as the sun.
sentences.n: “wenn … auch” is a concessive pair, ‘even if, although’; the auch here does not mean ‘also’.

sentences.t: Die Wanderer standen still und fragten einen Bauer, der mit seinem Wagen vorbei fuhr, was das für ein Licht sei.
sentences.l: The travellers stood still and asked a peasant, who was driving past with his cart, what kind of a light that was.
sentences.i: The travellers stopped and asked a peasant driving past with his cart what kind of light it was.
sentences.n: “was für ein …” = what sort of a …; the für in this frame is not ‘for’. “sei” is the subjunctive of reported speech — the tale reports their question rather than quoting it, and German marks that with the verb form.

sentences.t: „Das ist der Mond,“ antwortete dieser, „unser Schultheiß hat ihn für drei Thaler gekauft und an den Eichbaum befestigt.
sentences.l: “That is the moon,” answered this one, “our village magistrate has bought it for three thalers and fastened it to the oak tree.
sentences.i: “That is the moon,” the man answered; “our bailiff bought it for three thalers and fastened it to the oak tree.
sentences.n: “dieser” — ‘this one’, meaning the person last named: a neat way of saying ‘the peasant’ without repeating him. The Schultheiß was the village headman, the lord’s appointed magistrate; here the moon is village property, bought and maintained like a street lamp.

sentences.t: Er muß täglich Öl aufgießen und ihn rein erhalten, damit er immer hell brennt.
sentences.l: He must pour on oil daily and keep it clean, so that it always burns brightly.
sentences.i: He has to pour on oil every day and keep it clean, so that it always burns brightly.
sentences.n: “ihn” is the moon — der Mond is masculine, so German says ‘him’ where English says ‘it’. “aufgießen” is separable (gießt auf), to pour on.

sentences.t: Dafür erhält er von uns wöchentlich einen Thaler.“
sentences.l: For that he receives from us a thaler weekly.
sentences.i: For that he gets a thaler a week from us.
sentences.n: The Thaler was a large silver coin; a thaler a week for tending the moon, against the three thalers it cost to buy — the tale keeps the village accounts straight.

sentences.t: Als der Bauer weggefahren war, sagte der eine von ihnen „diese Lampe könnten wir brauchen, wir haben daheim einen Eichbaum, der eben so groß ist, daran können wir sie hängen.
sentences.l: When the peasant had driven away, one of them said “this lamp we could use, we have an oak tree at home that is just as big, on it we can hang it.
sentences.i: When the peasant had driven off, one of them said: “We could use this lamp; we have an oak at home just as big, and we can hang it on that.
sentences.n: The speech runs straight on from “sagte” with no comma before the quotation — 1857 punctuation, which you will see all through. “eben so groß” = just as big (modern ebenso).

sentences.t: Was für eine Freude, wenn wir Nachts nicht in der Finsternis herum tappen!“
sentences.l: What a joy, when we do not grope about in the darkness at night!
sentences.i: What a joy, if we no longer had to grope about in the dark at night!
sentences.n: “Nachts” is an adverb, ‘at night’, though 1857 prints it with a capital. “herum tappen” — to grope around; modern spelling joins it into one word, herumtappen.

sentences.t: „Wißt ihr was?“ sprach der zweite, „wir wollen Wagen und Pferde holen und den Mond wegführen.
sentences.l: “Do you know what?” spoke the second, “we will fetch cart and horses and lead the moon away.
sentences.i: “Do you know what?” said the second. “Let us fetch a cart and horses and carry the moon off.
sentences.n: “wir wollen” is the ordinary German way of saying ‘let us’ — a proposal, not a statement of wanting. “Wißt” is the 1857 spelling of wisst.

sentences.t: Sie können sich hier einen andern kaufen.“
sentences.l: They can buy themselves another one here.
sentences.n: “sich … kaufen” — the dative reflexive marks who benefits from the buying; English simply says ‘buy’, so the sich disappears in translation.

sentences.t: „Ich kann gut klettern,“ sprach der dritte, „ich will ihn schon herunter holen.“
sentences.l: “I can climb well,” spoke the third, “I will fetch it down all right.”
sentences.i: “I am a good climber,” said the third; “I shall have it down, never fear.”
sentences.n: “schon” here is not ‘already’ but a particle of confidence — ‘I’ll manage it’. “herunter holen” is separable, holt herunter.

sentences.t: Der vierte brachte einen Wagen mit Pferden herbei, und der dritte stieg den Baum hinauf, bohrte ein Loch in den Mond, zog ein Seil hindurch und ließ ihn herab.
sentences.l: The fourth brought a cart with horses up, and the third climbed the tree up, bored a hole in the moon, drew a rope through it and let it down.
sentences.i: The fourth brought up a cart and horses, and the third climbed the tree, bored a hole in the moon, drew a rope through it and let it down.
sentences.n: Four actions in a row, each with its own little direction word at the clause end: herbei (hither), hinauf (up, away from us), hindurch (through), herab (down, toward us). German keeps them there; English folds them into the verb.

sentences.t: Als die glänzende Kugel auf dem Wagen lag, deckten sie ein Tuch darüber, damit niemand den Raub bemerken sollte.
sentences.l: When the gleaming globe lay on the cart, they spread a cloth over it, so that no one should notice the theft.
sentences.n: “Raub” is plain robbery, and the tale calls the deed what it is before moving cheerfully on. “sollte” in a damit-clause carries purpose: so that no one should notice.

sentences.t: Sie brachten ihn glücklich in ihr Land und stellten ihn auf eine hohe Eiche.
sentences.l: They brought it safely into their land and set it on a high oak.
sentences.i: They got it safely home to their own land and set it up on a tall oak.
sentences.n: “glücklich” here is not ‘happily’ but ‘successfully, without mishap’ — an older use that turns up often in these tales.

sentences.t: Alte und junge freuten sich, als die neue Lampe ihr Licht über alle Felder leuchten ließ und Stuben und Kammern damit erfüllte.
sentences.l: Old and young rejoiced when the new lamp let its light shine over all the fields and filled parlours and chambers with it.
sentences.i: Old and young were glad when the new lamp sent its light out over all the fields and filled parlours and chambers with it.
sentences.n: “Alte und junge” — adjectives standing as nouns, the old and the young; 1857 leaves junge in lower case. “leuchten ließ” is lassen + infinitive, ‘let (it) shine’.

sentences.t: Die Zwerge kamen aus den Felsenhöhlen hervor, und die kleinen Wichtelmänner tanzten in ihren rothen Röckchen auf den Wiesen den Ringeltanz.
sentences.l: The dwarves came forth out of the rock-caves, and the little brownies danced the ring-dance in their red coats on the meadows.
sentences.i: The dwarves came out of their caves in the rocks, and the little brownies in their red jackets danced their ring-dance on the meadows.
sentences.n: “Ringeltanz” is a round dance, danced in a ring. “rothen” is the 1857 spelling of roten; the small red jackets are the standing dress of the Wichtelmänner in these tales. The new light draws out the creatures who live below ground — the first hint that the moon belongs elsewhere.

sentences.t: Die vier versorgten den Mond mit Öl, putzten den Dacht und erhielten wöchentlich ihren Thaler.
sentences.l: The four supplied the moon with oil, trimmed the wick and received their thaler weekly.
sentences.i: The four kept the moon supplied with oil, trimmed the wick, and drew their thaler every week.
sentences.n: “Dacht” is the old form of Docht, the wick, and “putzen” of a lamp means to trim it, not to polish it. The four have quietly taken over the magistrate’s office, wage and all.

sentences.t: Aber sie wurden alte Greise, und als der eine erkrankte und seinen Tod voraus sah, verordnete er daß der vierte Theil des Mondes als sein Eigenthum ihm mit in das Grab sollte gegeben werden.
sentences.l: But they became old greybeards, and when the one fell ill and saw his death in advance, he ordered that the fourth part of the moon, as his property, should be given him along into the grave.
sentences.i: But they grew into old men, and when the first of them fell ill and saw his death coming, he directed that the fourth part of the moon, as his property, should go into the grave with him.
sentences.n: “verordnete” is the word used of a legal disposition — he is making his will, and a quarter of the moon is entered as property. At the end of the clause German stacks “sollte gegeben werden” in an order English cannot copy: should — given — be.

sentences.t: Als er gestorben war, stieg der Schultheiß auf den Baum und schnitt mit der Heckenscheere ein Viertel ab, das in den Sarg gelegt ward.
sentences.l: When he had died, the village magistrate climbed up the tree and cut a quarter off with the hedge-shears, which was laid in the coffin.
sentences.i: When he had died, the bailiff climbed the tree and cut a quarter off with the hedge-shears, and it was laid in the coffin.
sentences.n: “Heckenscheere” (modern Heckenschere) is the shears used for clipping hedges: the moon is pruned like a shrub. “ward” is the old past of werden, modern wurde — it will recur throughout this tale.

sentences.t: Das Licht des Mondes nahm ab, aber noch nicht merklich.
sentences.l: The light of the moon decreased, but not yet noticeably.
sentences.i: The moon’s light grew less, though not yet noticeably.
sentences.n: “abnehmen” (nahm ab) is the ordinary word for the waning of the moon — the tale is explaining the moon’s changing light as a series of burials.

sentences.t: Als der zweite starb, ward ihm das zweite Viertel mitgegeben und das Licht minderte sich.
sentences.l: When the second died, the second quarter was given along with him and the light lessened itself.
sentences.i: When the second died, the second quarter went into the grave with him, and the light grew less.
sentences.n: “mitgeben” — to give along, the standard word for what is put into the coffin with the dead. “sich mindern” is reflexive in German where English is simply intransitive: the light lessens itself.

sentences.t: Noch schwächer ward es nach dem Tod des dritten, der gleichfalls seinen Theil mitnahm, und als der vierte ins Grab kam, trat die alte Finsternis wieder ein.
sentences.l: Still weaker it became after the death of the third, who likewise took his part along, and when the fourth came into the grave, the old darkness set in again.
sentences.i: It grew weaker still after the death of the third, who likewise took his share with him, and when the fourth went into his grave the old darkness set in again.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with “Noch schwächer” and the finite verb “ward” follows immediately: whatever stands first, the verb comes second. “eintreten” (trat ein) is what a condition does when it begins.

sentences.t: Wenn die Leute Abends ohne Laterne ausgiengen, stießen sie mit den Köpfen zusammen.
sentences.l: When the people went out in the evening without a lantern, they knocked their heads together.
sentences.i: When people went out in the evening without a lantern, they knocked heads together.
sentences.n: “zusammen stoßen” — to collide. The picture is deadpan: the tale gives the collision as the plain consequence and says no more. “ausgiengen” is the 1857 spelling of ausgingen (ausgehen, separable aus-).

sentences.t: Als aber die Theile des Monds in der Unterwelt sich wieder vereinigten, so wurden dort, wo immer Dunkelheit geherrscht hatte, die Todten unruhig und erwachten aus ihrem Schlaf.
sentences.l: But when the parts of the moon united themselves again in the underworld, then there, where darkness had always reigned, the dead grew restless and awoke out of their sleep.
sentences.i: But when the parts of the moon came together again down in the underworld, then there, where darkness had always reigned, the dead grew restless and woke out of their sleep.
sentences.n: “Monds” is an older genitive of der Mond beside Mondes; both forms stand in this tale. The “so” after the long when-clause is not ‘so’ but a resumptive ‘then’, very common in 1857 prose.

sentences.t: Sie erstaunten als sie wieder sehen konnten: das Mondlicht war ihnen genug, denn ihre Augen waren so schwach geworden, daß sie den Glanz der Sonne nicht ertragen hätten.
sentences.l: They were astonished when they could see again: the moonlight was enough for them, for their eyes had become so weak that they would not have borne the brilliance of the sun.
sentences.i: They were astonished when they could see again; the moonlight was enough for them, for their eyes had grown so weak that they could not have borne the brilliance of the sun.
sentences.n: “hätten … ertragen” is the past subjunctive of a supposed case — ‘would not have been able to bear it’, with the modal simply left out, as German often does.

sentences.t: Sie erhoben sich, wurden lustig und nahmen ihre alte Lebensweise wieder an.
sentences.l: They raised themselves up, became merry and took their old way of life up again.
sentences.i: They rose up, grew merry, and took up their old way of life again.
sentences.n: “annehmen” (nahmen … an) is separable, and the particle an waits at the very end, behind the adverb wieder.

sentences.t: Ein Theil gieng zum Spiel und Tanz, andere liefen in die Wirthshäuser, wo sie Wein forderten, sich betranken, tobten und zankten, und endlich ihre Knüttel aufhoben und sich prügelten.
sentences.l: One part went to gaming and dancing, others ran into the inns, where they called for wine, got themselves drunk, raged and quarrelled, and finally raised their cudgels and thrashed one another.
sentences.i: Some went off to gaming and dancing, others ran into the inns, where they called for wine, drank themselves drunk, raged and quarrelled, and at last took up their cudgels and set about one another.
sentences.n: “Knüttel” (modern Knüppel) is a heavy stick, a cudgel. Nothing here is softened: the dead take up exactly the life they had, brawl and all.

sentences.t: Der Lärm ward immer ärger und drang endlich bis in den Himmel hinauf.
sentences.l: The noise became ever worse and pressed at last up as far as into heaven.
sentences.i: The din grew worse and worse and reached at last right up into heaven.
sentences.n: “immer ärger” — ever worse; immer with a comparative is German’s ‘more and more’. “drang … hinauf” is dringen, to press or force its way, with the direction word hinauf at the end.

sentences.t: Der heil. Petrus, der das Himmelsthor bewacht, glaubte die Unterwelt wäre in Aufruhr gerathen und rief die himmlischen Heerschaaren zusammen, die den bösen Feind, wenn er mit seinen Gesellen den Aufenthalt der Seligen stürmen wollte, zurück jagen sollten.
sentences.l: The holy Peter, who guards the gate of heaven, believed the underworld had fallen into uproar and called the heavenly hosts together, which were to drive back the evil enemy if he should want to storm the dwelling of the blessed with his fellows.
sentences.i: St. Peter, who keeps the gate of heaven, thought the underworld had risen in revolt, and called the heavenly hosts together to drive back the evil enemy, should he and his fellows try to storm the dwelling-place of the blessed.
sentences.n: “heil.” is the abbreviation of heilig, holy: der heilige Petrus, St. Peter. “bewacht” stands in the present tense inside a past story — he guards that gate still. “wäre … gerathen” is the subjunctive of reported thought: this is what Peter believed, not what the tale asserts. “der böse Feind” is a standing name for the devil.

sentences.t: Da sie aber nicht kamen, so setzte er sich auf sein Pferd und ritt durch das Himmelsthor hinab in die Unterwelt.
sentences.l: But since they did not come, he set himself on his horse and rode down through the gate of heaven into the underworld.
sentences.i: But as they did not come, he mounted his horse and rode down through the gate of heaven into the underworld.
sentences.n: “Da” at the head of a clause is causal here, ‘since, as’, not ‘there’ — the next sentence begins with the other Da. “setzte sich” is the reflexive German uses for seating oneself.

sentences.t: Da brachte er die Todten zur Ruhe, hieß sie sich wieder in die Gräber legen und nahm den Mond mit fort, den er oben am Himmel aufhieng.
sentences.l: There he brought the dead to rest, bade them lay themselves in the graves again and took the moon away with him, which he hung up above in the sky.
sentences.i: There he brought the dead to rest, bade them lie down in their graves again, and carried the moon off with him, and hung it up above in the sky.
sentences.n: This “Da” is the other one — ‘there, thereupon’. “hieß” with a bare infinitive is the old ‘bade (someone) do’. “aufhieng” is the 1857 spelling of aufhing (aufhängen); with it the tale arrives at what it set out to explain, why the moon hangs where it does.

glossary.bewacht: bewachen — guards, keeps watch over (3rd sg. present: ‘der das Himmelsthor bewacht’)
glossary.dabei: dabei — by it, by that light (‘dabei sehen’ = to see by it); also: present, there alongside
glossary.erfüllte: erfüllen — filled (3rd sg. past: ‘Stuben und Kammern damit erfüllte’ = filled parlours and chambers with it)
glossary.erhalten: erhalten — to keep, to maintain (infinitive: ‘ihn rein erhalten’ = keep it clean); the same verb elsewhere means to receive
glossary.heil: heilig — holy (abbreviated ‘heil.’ before a saint’s name: der heil. Petrus = St. Peter)
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, told, ordered (3rd sg. past, with a bare infinitive); also “was called”
glossary.putzten: putzen — trimmed (3rd pl. past; of a lamp, ‘den Dacht putzen’ = to trim the wick, not to polish)
glossary.schlaf: der Schlaf — sleep (‘aus ihrem Schlaf’ = out of their sleep); not the imperative of schlafen
glossary.schon: schon — a particle of confidence here, ‘right enough, never fear’ (‘ich will ihn schon herunter holen’); elsewhere: already
glossary.trat: eintreten — set in, began (3rd sg. past; separable ein-, the particle waiting at the clause end: ‘trat … wieder ein’)
glossary.unruhig: unruhig — restless, uneasy (plain High German here: ‘die Todten unruhig’ = the dead grew restless)
glossary.ärger: arg — worse (comparative of arg, ‘bad’: ‘immer ärger’ = worse and worse); not der Ärger, vexation
